questions.question: Explain how India became a British colony and describe two conditions in India that encouraged people to sign indenture contracts.
questions.expected_answer: The East India Company, founded in 1600, set up trading posts at Madras, Bombay and Calcutta, then used its armies of sepoys to take territory as the Mughal Empire weakened, beginning with victory at Plassey in 1757. After the uprising of 1857, the British government abolished Company rule in 1858 and ruled India directly; in 1877 Victoria became Empress of India. Conditions: high land revenue and debt led many farmers to lose their land; hand-weavers lost work to machine-made British cloth; repeated droughts and famines, such as those of the late 1870s, killed millions; dense populations and landlessness; some wished to escape caste restrictions or family conflict.

questions.question: Why did Natal's sugar planters bring labourers from India rather than employing local African workers?
questions.expected_answer: Sugar was labour-intensive: cane had to be planted, weeded and cut by hand and crushed quickly at harvest, so planters needed many reliable, cheap workers for the whole season. Most Zulu-speaking people in Natal had access to land in locations and could support themselves; men worked for wages only for short periods to pay the hut tax or buy cattle; field cultivation was largely women's work; and Shepstone's system reduced pressure on them to work for settlers. The shortage was really one of workers willing to accept low wages and long contracts. Mauritius and Caribbean colonies already used Indian indentured labour, and indenture let employers punish labourers who left. Natal passed laws in 1859, and the Truro arrived in November 1860.

questions.question: Describe the main terms of an indenture contract in Natal and the process of recruitment and travel.
questions.expected_answer: From 1864 the contract lasted five years, with one employer; wages began at 10 shillings a month and rose by 1 shilling a month each year to 14 shillings in the fifth year; food rations, housing and medical care were provided. After five years of indenture and five more years in Natal, a free return passage to India was offered, with land grants available instead in the early years. Licensed recruiters and agents toured villages, markets and stations; some recruits chose freely, others were misled. Recruits went to depots in Madras or Calcutta for medical checks and a magistrate's check; at least 40 women for every 100 men were required. The voyage took about four to eight weeks in crowded ships with disease risk; on arrival the Protector registered them and allocated them to employers.
